Head coach | highlights = * [[NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year]] (1996) * First-team [[All-Pro]] ([[2000 All-Pro Team|2000]]) * Second-team All-Pro ([[1999 All-Pro Team|1999]]) * 4× [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1998 Pro Bowl|1997]]–[[2001 Pro Bowl|2000]]) * [[Tennessee Titans#Titans Ring of Honor|Titans/Oilers Ring of Honor]] * [[Tennessee Titans#Retired numbers|Tennessee Titans No. 27]] retired * [[Heisman Trophy]] (1995) * [[List of unanimous All-Americans in college football|Unanimous All-American]] ([[1995 College Football All-America Team|1995]]) * [[Big Ten Male Athlete of the Year]] (1996) * [[Ohio State Buckeyes football#Retired numbers|Ohio State Buckeyes No. 27]] retired * [[Big South–OVC Football Association|Big South–OVC]] Coach of the Year (2024) | statlabel1 = [[Rushing yards]] | statvalue1 = 10,441 | statlabel2 = [[Rushing average]] | statvalue2 = 3.6 | statlabel3 = [[Touchdown|Rushing touchdowns]] | statvalue3 = 68 | statlabel4 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Receptions]] | statvalue4 = 268 | statlabel5 = [[Receiving yards]] | statvalue5 = 2,227 | statlabel6 = [[Touchdown|Receiving touchdowns]] | statvalue6 = 10 | regular_record = {{Winning percentage|28|29|record=y}} | playoff_record = {{Winning percentage|0|1|record=y}} | overall_record = {{Winning percentage|28|30|record=y}} | pfr = GeorEd00 | CollegeHOF = 2267 }} '''Edward Nathan George Jr.''' (born September 24, 1973) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former [[running back]] who is currently the head coach at [[Bowling Green Falcons football|Bowling Green State University]]. He previously served as the head coach of the [[Tennessee State Tigers football|Tennessee State University]] from 2021 to 2024. George played [[college football]] for [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State University]] from [[1992 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|1992]] to [[1995 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|1995]]. He played professionally in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for nine seasons from 1996 to 2004, primarily for the [[Tennessee Titans]] franchise. George was born in [[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania. He attended [[Abington Senior High School]] until the 10th grade and then transferred to [[Fork Union Military Academy]]. George enrolled at [[Ohio State University]] and played running back for the Buckeyes, starting for two seasons. As a senior in 1995, he led Ohio State to the [[1996 Florida Citrus Bowl|Florida Citrus Bowl]] and won the [[Heisman Trophy]]. George was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2011 as a player,{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=6558995 |title=Deion Sanders, Lloyd Carr join Eddie George in Hall's Class of '11 |website=[[ESPN]] |date=May 17, 2011 |access-date=December 1, 2016}} and the [[International Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2020.{{cite web |title=2020 International Sports Hall of Fame Inductees |url=https://sportshof.org/2020-hall-of-fame/ |website=www.sportshof.org |author=Dr. Robert Goldman | date=March 10, 2020 | access-date=July 14, 2023}} The [[Houston Oilers]] selected George in the first round (14th overall) of the [[1996 NFL draft]]. He played nine seasons as a running back in the NFL, with the Tennessee Titans (both in Tennessee and in Houston when the franchise was known as the Houston Oilers) and [[Dallas Cowboys]] for a single season in 2004. George became a starter immediately upon joining the Oilers. In 1999, after the franchise moved to Tennessee, he led the Titans to an appearance in [[Super Bowl XXXIV]], was selected to the [[1999 Pro Bowl|Pro Bowl]], and was honored as a second-team All-Pro. After football, George earned an MBA from [[Northwestern University]]'s [[Kellogg School of Management]]. In 2015, he guest-starred on an episode of the [[IFC (American TV channel)|IFC]] satirical talk show ''[[Comedy Bang! Bang! (TV series)|Comedy Bang! Bang!]]'', titled "Eddie George Wears a Navy Suit and Half-Zip Pullover." The following year, George appeared on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] in the musical ''[[Chicago (musical)|Chicago]]'' as the hustling lawyer [[Billy Flynn (Chicago)|Billy Flynn]].{{cite web|author=Mike Freeman |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2585491-mike-freemans-10-point-stance-eddie-georges-incredible-2nd-act |title=Mike Freeman's 10-Point Stance: Eddie George's Incredible 2nd Act |publisher=[[Bleacher Report]] |access-date=December 1, 2016}}

'''Paul Edward Brown''' (born February 19, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Cleveland Browns]], the [[Washington Redskins]], and the [[Los Angeles Rams]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]].

Brown attended Marion County High School in Jasper, Tennessee, and graduated in 1970.  At the [[University of Tennessee]], he was a safety and [[punt return]]er.  In 1973, he was [[Captain (sports)|team captain]] as a senior and was a first-team [[All-America]] selection by Football News.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://utsports.com/football/article.aspx?id=12180 |title=UTSPORTS.COM - University of Tennessee Athletics - Football |access-date=December 25, 2007 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130208221550/http://utsports.com/football/article.aspx?id=12180 |archive-date=February 8, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Brown was [[NFL draft|drafted]] by the Cleveland Browns in the eighth round of the [[1974 NFL draft]].  He was traded to the Washington Redskins during the 1975 season, and was an [[All-Pro]] and [[Pro Bowl]] selection during the [[1976 Washington Redskins season|1976]] and [[1977 Washington Redskins season|1977]] seasons.  In 1976, he led the National Football League in punt return yardage with 646 and was second in yards per return at 13.5.  He also had a 71-yard return for a touchdown that season.  In 1977, he led the NFL in punt returns with 57. On October 9, [[1977 Washington Redskins season|1977]], his 11 punt returns against the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] set an [[National Football League|NFL]] single-game record.<ref>Chick, Bob. "A Record To Kick About". ''St. Petersburg Evening Independent''. October 10, 1977</ref>

Traded to the Los Angeles Rams in 1978 for offensive lineman [[Jeff Williams (offensive lineman)|Jeff Williams]], Brown played that season and 1979 for the Rams.

In 1979 the Rams won the [[NFC Championship Game|National Football Conference championship]] and played the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in [[Super Bowl XIV]] on January 20, 1980.  Brown had an [[interception]] in the third quarter, but Pittsburgh won, 31-19.

Brown returned to professional football in 1983 with the [[Chicago Blitz]] of the [[United States Football League]].  He had six interceptions, including one returned for a touchdown, that season.<ref>[http://www.oursportscentral.com/usfl/stat83chi.htm USFL Site - 1983 United States Football League Stats]</ref>  He played for the USFL's [[Arizona Wranglers]] in 1984 and had two interceptions.<ref>[http://www.oursportscentral.com/usfl/stat84az.htm USFL Site - 1984 United States Football Stats]</ref>

Brown was inducted into the Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame in 2002.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://tshf.net/halloffame/brown-eddie/ | title=Brown, Eddie « Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame }}</ref>

'''Edward William Muransky''' (born January 20, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] for the [[Los Angeles Raiders]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Orlando Renegades]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). After retiring from football he became a business partner and advisor to [[Edward J. DeBartolo Jr.]], former [[San Francisco 49ers]] owner.  Muransky testified in the March 2000 trial of [[Louisiana]] [[Governor]] [[Edwin Edwards]], mainly about what DeBartolo had confided to Muransky. DeBartolo was the only [[extortion]] victim who claimed to have been extorted directly by Edwards, but Muransky could not provide direct testimony about private meetings between DeBartolo and Edwards. Muransky has continued to pursue business interests even after the controversies about DeBartolo have waned.
